utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-95-9-T, The Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall proceed with rejoinder arguments. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Yesterday, Mr. Weiner said, it's at page 19 of yesterday's transcript -- he quoted Prosecution witness, star Witness Todorovic, as saying "Dr. Simic was the person who had the authority in Samac." Transcript 10230. This is a misleading reference taken out of context. Just a few sentences after this, as the Prosecution further pressed Todorovic about Dr. Simic's so-called power and authority, Todorovic explained that, I quote: "It's a matter of interpretation." Again, if I remember - she, meaning Ms. Nancy Paterson - so "she asked me whether Mr. Blagoje Simic enjoyed authority among the people. And I said: Yes, he did, in the sense that people respected him." Todorovic continued saying that, I'm quoting: "What I meant was that he was in a good standing with the people." Same page, 10230. He repeated this sentiment again at transcript 10231. Todorovic even further admitted that he did not know whether Dr. Simic had the legal authority to issue orders. This hardly establishes that Dr. Simic was, I'm quoting, "powerful leader" as Mr. Weiner made him out to be. With regard to the so-called authority of Dr. Simic to appoint military commanders, the Defence reiterates its submission in its brief, paras 596, 478, and 639. The Trial Chamber heard testimony from several witnesses who confirmed that the appointment of military officials is under the authority of the superior military command, not civilian municipal officials. In our particular case, the superior commander was the 17th corps under the command of Colonel Dencic. This is also consistent with the laws and chain of command of Republika Srpska army. It is absurd to suggest that the municipal functionary would have the authority to appoint Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, as a commander of 2nd Posavina brigade. Several Defence witnesses gave evidence that the appointment of military commander at brigade level was under the authority of superior military command, which in our case was the east Bosnian corps under the command of Colonel Dencic. For example, Simeon Simic, transcript 13275-6; Dusan Tanasic, transcript 13759; Savo Popovic, transcript 16263. In addition, Your Honours, Witness Maksim Simeunovic, assistant commander for intelligence of the 17th Tactical Group gave evidence, it's transcript 15916, that Colonel Dencic had arrived at the command post bringing the order on appointment and promotion of Crni as the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. He greeted Crni in a good way, and they addressed each other as best man, in B/C/S "kum," which is English meaning of best man. Colonel Dencic and Crni. Also assistant commander for intelligence gave evidence that former commander of 2nd Posavina Brigade, Colonel Mico Djurdjevic, at that time was promoted to the higher position as the commander of larger military unit based in Brcko, and that was 1st Posavina Brigade. Transcript 15953-55. Again, the star witness for the Prosecution, Mr. Todorovic, gave evidence, it's at transcript 10236, that Colonel Dencic, commander of the East Bosnian Corps pursuant to his authority, pursuant to his military position, his power as a command of superior unit, appointed Crni. Further Todorovic testified that during the meeting in Ugljevik, former commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, Colonel Mico Djurdjevic expressed his opinion that, and I'm quoting the word of the star witness of the Prosecution, what Colonel Djurdjevic said at that occasion: "I think it is better for Crni to be a commander because soldiers were in awe of him and would follow him." Two Colonels speaking on the occasion of the meeting at the East Bosnian Corps command. They are shouting -- they speaking as colleagues on military issues, appointments and other matters. Todorovic testified that the commander of East Bosnian Corps had made the decision of appointment on his own and in accordance with his authority as a superior military commander. With regard to Exhibit P115 and P117, as well as P127, the Defence reiterates its position expressed in its brief, in the light of the fact that the tensions between army and civilian authorities were commonly known throughout the wartime period in Republika Srpska and in the light of the fact that the Prosecution during trial proceedings firmly opposed work, decisions, and judgements of military courts or martial courts of Republika Srpska, it is clear that this Trial Chamber should not attach any weight to this exhibit since in this case, the Prosecution obviously contradicts itself. On one side, they are in favour of certain work of military courts of Republika Srpska, but on the other side, when no Serbs were sentenced, were under the procedure of the same courts, same military courts of Republika Srpska, it's illegitimate. It's a kangaroo court. It's a mock trial. Another issue, with regard to the issue of the presence of Dr. Simic in the months following his medical treatment after he was wounded by the end of July, the Defence emphasised that Dr. Simic was significantly unable to perform his duties, and only occasionally he participated in meetings with various officials. We explained that in our brief in details. In any case, there is nothing to suggest that Dr. Simic was involved in any criminal activity throughout the period covered by the indictment. There is no evidence to that extent. And we clearly stated and substantiated on several occasions during final brief and closing arguments. With respect to the Prosecution Exhibit P128, the Defence reiterates its position stated in our final brief. It's at page 170. And emphasise that the document which is neither signed nor stamped, bears no probative value. Not to mention that the Prosecution failed to establish the chain of custody regarding this document, and that there is no evidence or testimony which would prove beyond reasonable doubt that this document was ever received, discussed, or implemented in the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Especially keeping in mind destruction of all means of communication at that time between Samac municipal authorities and the republican level. This particular submission is related to the procedural issues, namely the issue of the weight of the evidence. But assuming the -- of this particular exhibit existed, first of all, each case should be viewed on the basis of its specificity and in accordance with the evidence and facts in each particular case. One exhibit cannot be sufficient for the determination of the case in totality. So which conclusions can be drawn with regard to Defence case in respect to this document? It is clear that the republican level authorities intended to limit the competencies of the Crisis Staff to nonmilitary and nonpolice functions. In particular, in paragraph 1 in this document, we can find the basis, the legislation basis that the Crisis Staff actually are municipal assemblies throughout the period of war when the Municipal Assemblies cannot be convened. So in addition, there is overwhelming evidence shown that the Crisis Staff in Samac was varied and diverse. We have evidences to that extent. In Samac, for example, the evidence shows that different professionals from all walks of life participated in the Crisis Staff when problems concerning their field of expertise arose. Waterworks, power supply, medical care, organisation of the work in companies, in public state companies, economy in wartime, et cetera, et cetera. We heard many evidences to that extent. Another point I would like to make is the clear distinction between civilian authorities and military and police, in terms of command authority. The Prosecution wants to portray Dr. Simic ass having control or authority over the military and police in Samac municipality. The evidence does not bear this out. The Prosecution claims the republican government directed the Crisis Staff to, inter alia, prevent looting and war profiteering, the maltreatment of prisoners of war, and to provide for the safety of the population, for the property. The Prosecution's interpretation of this document is erroneous. The evidence overwhelming shows that these were areas over which the police and military had control before, during, and after the conflict. Further, this so-called directive explicitly stated that "the command of the TO and police forces is under the exclusive authority of the professional staff," which means military and police officers. "And therefore, any interference regarding the command of the TO and/or the use of the police forces must be prevented." In addition, the case law of this Tribunal, Your Honours, and international law in general clearly established the responsibility of the military and police with regard to the law and order, the safety of the population, the protection of property, and the treatment of prisoners of war. Article 86, 87 of additional protocols, then we have a hostage case, we have the Blaskic case within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, Krstic case, that's a well-established issue, the role and responsibility of the military commander within his zone of responsibility. Assistant commander for intelligence for 17th Tactical Group, Maksim Simeunovic, a witness for Simo Zaric and his superior, testified that Colonel Nikolic, commander of 17th Tactical Group, state at meeting with the municipal officials, and I'm quoting: "He wanted to have the situation under his control within his area of responsibility." He said that he would prevent lootings that did take place, and he asked for support and he received that, I'm underlining, support from the persons who were present at that meeting. Not orders. Colonel Nikolic did not receive orders or instructions. That's transcript 15911. Obviously Colonel Nikolic, an experienced and well-trained officer, as well as a commander of 7.000 soldiers in the area, knew which responsibilities were his and which belonged to the Crisis Staff, to civilian authorities. The evidence in this case, Your Honours, clearly shows that the Crisis Staff's role was the same as the municipal assembly. In terms of economic issues and the other aspect of life, it is clear that the Executive Board, not the Crisis Staff, was in charge. In sum, what did the Crisis Staff have authority over? The police? No. The military? No. The POWs? No. The Executive Board? No. Economic activity? No. Yesterday, our learned colleague Mr. Re stated that the Prosecution never suggested that the SDS is a joint criminal enterprise or that the SDS is a criminal organisation. The Defence agrees with Mr. Re. Needless to mention that at this time, a member of collective presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and actually copresident, because there are three copresidents from three constituent people from Bosnia sitting as members of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so at this particular time, Your Honours, the member of SDS party from Republika Srpska is a head of state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. His name is Mr. Paravac, a member and candidate of SDS. 13 years after the establishment of the SDS, this party was never banned, this party was never accused as a criminal organisation, and still - I'm not speaking on behalf of this party, no parties at all - and still this party enjoys a great support in the voters' body of Republika Srpska and elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let me remind you that at this particular moment, HDZ, SDA, and SDS formed three members presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, hopefully, I believe that all responsible top political leaders learned something from the recent history and as we know that in 1992, all three parties were also sharing power. So I hope with a little friendship of international forces, nothing serious will happen. But that's just for the record. However, the Defence feels it necessary to refresh Mr. Re's memory with regard to some words that he used yesterday. In the opening statement made by his colleague, Mr. Di Fazio, that was in September 2001, Mr. Re was not with us at that time. So Mr. Di Fazio used the very words the Prosecution used to begin its case. Mr. Di Fazio often placed the blame squarely on the SDS. He said, for example, that the SDS began to make plans regarding the creation of separate Serb state within Bosnia. This is at transcript 927. Then, through the SDS policy of ethnic cleansing, he clearly stated that these were the acts of the SDS. Mr. Di Fazio did not use the word "some members of the SDS" or "other people," as Mr. Re stated yesterday. And needless to remind you, Your Honours, and all participants in this case with which force, how fiercely the Prosecution cross-examined the witnesses especially of Simo Zaric witnesses, military officials, political opponents of Dr. Simic and the SDS with regard to the same issue, the SDS did that, the SDS did this, et cetera, et cetera. We have everything on the transcript. Again, in the fifth amended indictment in paragraphs 23 and 24, his superior, superior of Mr. Re, his superior, Deputy Prosecutor Graham Blewitt stated "the SDS" - again, not"certain members of the SDS," or other people - "and the JNA worked on the creation of separate Serb municipalities through the means of ethnic cleansing." Moreover, the Prosecution seeks to downplay its sudden shift from the use of term "acting in concert together" in its five indictments and throughout the trial to the more comprehensive term "joint criminal enterprise" in its final trial brief and in final oral arguments. The Prosecution disingenuously states that the Defence should have known that the Prosecution meant joint criminal enterprise when it used the term "acting in concert with others." However, the OTP has been specifically using the concept and term joint criminal enterprise in detail in no less than 17 indictments dating back to 1991 -- 1999. 1999. And dated back to 1999. And now, at the end of two years of these proceedings, the Prosecution justifies this sudden switch to simply employing a term more recently preferred by the Tribunal, but the OTP has been using the term "joint criminal enterprise" for the past four years, and yet the Prosecution did not mention this term, this concept, over the past two years of this trial, until the last month of proceedings. At the minimum, this lack of persistence in terminology coming so late in this case creates unnecessary confusion. The Prosecution dismissed the Defence claim that switching such vital terminology at this late stage introduces vagueness and ambiguity by arguing that the Defence should have raised that issue after the indictment was amended. Well, again, Mr. Re, since he was not there at that time, he forgets that the Defence did raise this issue when it objected to the use of the term "acting in concert together" and other terms in its opposition, in its objections to the form of the fourth amended indictment. While the Trial Chamber did the introduction of this term, it also stated it was limited to count 1. In fact, this Honourable Trial Chamber, at several points in its decision on the Prosecution motion to amend the indictment, this decision was rendered on the 20 December 2001, expressed concerns over the lack of precision of terms used by the Prosecution, such as "including among others" this is paragraph 10 of said decision. And then, I'm quoting, "including but not limited to." This is paragraph 12 of said decision. And then what this Honourable Trial Chamber said which create "possible confusion in the indictment." It was said in paragraph 19. Specifically this Honourable Trial Chamber concluded that "the use of such imprecise and ambiguous terms, particularly when used in relation to material facts, including the underlying facts upon which the Prosecution charge is based, do not provide the accused with sufficient notice of the nature of the case they have to answer." This is in paragraph 10. Finally, "the chronic lack of specificity used by the Prosecution prompted this Honourable Trial Chamber to find that many of the issues raised are due to the lack of diligence on the part of the Prosecution." This is paragraph 29. In sum, the Defence has submitted that the terms "acting in concert together" and "joint criminal enterprise" are not interchangeable. Neither Judge Hunt, nor any of the Trial Chamber within this Honourable Tribunal have used these terms interchangeably. To switch these terms so late in the game creates confusion and introduces uncertainty as to the precise nature of the allegation the Defence was to defend against. Lastly, due to the limited time for this oral submission, the Defence respectfully directs the Trial Chamber to its final brief and its final oral argument for the basis of the Defence position. And another matter of sort of imprecision, maybe I'm wrong, but in paragraph 23 of the indictment, fifth amended indictment, there is a sentence "the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as an independent" - I'm underlining- "nation by the United States and countries of the European community as of 7th of April, 1992." As I said, maybe it's a matter of language, but what is the difference between Bosnia-Herzegovina as a nation and Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state? We lawyers sometimes are so -- we are pursuing and we are trying to split a hair on two, and as I said, maybe it's a kind of imprecision, but I will leave it. Yesterday, the Prosecution again raised the issue of the international armed conflict, pages 30 and 31 of the yesterday's transcript, and appears to again invite the Trial Chamber to take judicial notice thereof. With regard to the Defence submission related to the findings of the Badinter commission, opinion number 2, paragraph 2, "the basis for changing the findings the commission are the following, the commission referred to the Serb people in B and H as a minority," that is a word used by Badinter commission in paragraph 2 of its opinion number 2. When until that finding, Serb people in Bosnia were considered as a full constituent nation, same as Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. This word is problematic. Number two, the Dayton Peace Accords reaffirm the right of Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a full constituent nation, not a minority. Number 3, following the general principles of law, pacta sum servanda, the Dayton Peace Accords should be viewed as a source of international law, and therefore the findings of the Badinter commission are irrelevant and, in fact, annulled. Although the Defence would prefer to use its limited time to address other matters, it is compelled to once again respond to our colleagues from the OTP by directing them to the decision of the Pre-trial Chamber in this case on the 25 of March of 1999, to which the Defence has already referred. Namely, in this decision, the Trial Chamber rejected the Prosecution request to take judicial notice on the international character of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, emphasising on page 5 that Rule 94 is intended to cover facts and not legal consequences inferred from them. And that the Trial Chamber can only take judicial notice of factual findings, but not a legal characterisation as such. I have one copy, so maybe after the break, I can give to my learned friends, of the decision in this particular case rendered by that Trial Chamber Judge May, Judge Benouna, and Judge Robinson. In addition, the Prosecution mostly refers to paragraph 85 of our joint statement of matters which are not in dispute, filed on 27 of April, 2001, and yes, in this paragraph, the Defence indeed concedes that an armed conflict was taking place in Bosnia and Herzegovina between May and December 1992. But, Your Honours, this is not the point. The question is whether the conflict was international in character, and as I said, which is a requisite element of application of Article 2 of the Statute. The said paragraph 85 specifically refers to an armed conflict only in the context of the requirement of Article 3, common to the four Geneva Conventions of 1949. And Article 3 does not require as a prerequisite element that the conflict be international. So in sum, the Defence submits that such misleading reference by the Prosecution are nothing more than a waste of precious time of this Honourable Trial Chamber's, and the Defence hereby affirms its belief that this is a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide. In its submission on the Prosecution's stated that the municipality of Bosanski Samac remained a part of both Seselj indictment and Stanisic and Simatovic indictment, the Defence acknowledges that these two indictments include factual basis of the events in Bosanski Samac. However, the same Office of the Prosecution, and in this particular case, what our friends made reference, this was really another unconstructive reference on the Prosecution part because neither of these indictments, Your Honours, contains charges under Article 2, but only under Article 3 of the Statute. It speaks for itself. Their indictments speak for themselves. Issue regarding Simo Zaric book. Your Honours, Zaric himself, the author, codefendant, stated that this was an inaccurate representation of events. The other persons wrote this book, and he was not under control, et cetera. Due to that fact, this particular book, Simo Zaric book, I believe it's P180, is absolutely without any weight. Zaric is not a legal expert, and he is not qualified to pontificate on whether the events in Bosanski Samac amounted to ethnic cleansing or any other form of crime known to Statute of the Tribunal and international humanitarian law. The testimony of Zaric should be cautiously considered when it comes to Dr. Simic, because Zaric was a political opponent of Dr. Simic and had a motive to fabricate events in order to deflect the blame from himself in some parts. With regard to Variant A and B, as for the Variant A and B which is Exhibit P3, the Prosecution has repeatedly referred to in an attempt to establish the critical link that they need between Bosanski Samac civilian authorities and the SDS top leadership. Rather than bolstering their argument with hard facts, the Prosecution simply reiterates the same tired story. Since the Prosecution in fact cites only this unauthenticated and unsigned piece paper, the Defence is compelled to respectfully direct the Trial Chamber's attention to the relevant facts reached in this particular case, including, inter alia, the following: Number one, the Prosecution itself has admitted that unable to produce a copy of this phantom exhibit that was supposedly sent to Bosanski Samac. No evidence to that extent. The Defence submits the reason for this is that it simply does not exist. Number two, even the highest organ of Republika Srpska SDS explicitly denied the existence of the said document. I'm quoting word document. This is Defence Exhibit D23/1. Stating "the main board as well as any other SDS body never considered or instructed the organisation and activation of the Serb people in B and H at its session. And that "such instructions were given by a certain number of retired officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army, JNA." That's Exhibit D23/1. Number 3, as it obvious from Prosecution Exhibit P124, the preamble of the decision of the establishment of the Assembly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Pantelic please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, can you slow down. The interpreters have to get every word.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do my best, Your Honour, because my situation is always a race against time. I do apologise to interpreters. As is obvious from Prosecution Exhibit P124, the preamble on the decision on the establishment of the assembly of the Serb people of the municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo explicitly states that the creation of the assembly was based on the recommendation on the formation of the municipal assemblies of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This particular recommendation was a legitimate decision of an legitimate organ, namely People's Assembly of Republika Srpska, so this decision was adopted by the national assembly of Republika Srpska, not pursuant to Variant A and B, Bosanski Samac municipality was not formed pursuant to Variant A and B, but simply pursuant to the recommendation, and the decision which was published in Official Gazette of Republika Srpska, number 1/92. And like all other legislation from the republican level, it was not a secret document. It was not an illegitimate document, but rather was an open and public decision. Everyone can read Official Gazette of Republika Srpska number 1/92. And it is in preamble of Exhibit P124. We could find it. Legal basis. Plebiscite of Serbian people, recommendation which is a decision of Serbian legitimate assembly, national assembly, and principles for self-determination of the nation, Your Honours. In addition, the decision of the republican parliament are binding on municipalities, including Bosanski Samac. The Prosecution failed to produce a single witness who would actually say "yes, the Municipal Assembly in Bosanski Samac acted pursuant to this document, A and B variant." No evidence to that extent. Further, the Prosecution could not even produce a witness who even saw this alleged quoting document, phantom document, anywhere in Bosanski Samac. On the contrary, several witnesses, including Dr. Simic, testified that they had never seen or discussed this document let alone implemented it. And again, Your Honours, this is because the document does not exist. And in fact, there is no evidence besides the Prosecution's desperate, inferential leaps which would contain the acts of the municipal organs with this document. The link simply is not there. Paragraph 3 of the so-called phantom document, paragraph 3 of Variant B, which is dated 19 December 1991 calls for the immediate formation of Crisis Staff by the SDS. However, it is an uncontested fact that the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac was not then established by the SDS and did not consist only of members of the SDS. As stated in Defence oral submission of 1st July, the Defence and in our brief included several members of other parties, you remember, socialist party, liberal party, reformist, et cetera, and even no party memberships. Moreover, it was not established until five months on 19 April 1992, after hostilities had broken out in the municipality and after, Your Honours, an analogous Crisis Staff has been formed by the SDA and HDZ headed -- this joint Crisis Staff headed by top-ranking Croat and Muslim political leaders of the municipality of Samac. It was testified by codefendant Zaric, transcript 19125, and it is not in dispute in this case. And many other Defence witnesses. And, Your Honours, further Defence Exhibit D43/1 clearly establishes military and political objectives of municipal chapters, Samac municipal chapters, HDS [sic], HDZ, Crisis Staff, Croat Crisis Staff, which were implemented through formation of Croat Muslim municipality of Bosanski Samac Domeljevac on 17th of April, 1992, in partition of the territory of Bosanski Samac municipality. Just few words about this exhibit D43/1: Throughout the process of disclosure, the Prosecution, Your Honours, the Prosecution provided this document to the Defence. That's their document, Your Honours. And during the Prosecution case, they did not tender these documents into evidence. I know why. It is because this exhibit is devastating for the Prosecution case. The truth is only one, Your Honours. The truth of Samac case is that the Croat/Muslim leadership in Samac planned well in advance partition of the municipality on the ethnic grounds, and now we have the situation in accordance with the Croat and Muslim plan. And furthermore, in her plea agreement Ms. Plavsic never mentioned or referred to Bosanski Samac in any manner whatsoever. So this agreement that the Defence submits is entirely irrelevant for these proceedings and should therefore be disregarded by this Trial Chamber. Another unfounded theory of the Prosecution concerns the relationship of SDS and JNA in Samac municipality. The Defence will not waste its time on this. It merely would like to respectfully direct the Trial Chamber's attention to portion of the Defence brief, namely paragraphs 215, 251, 506 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Otherwise the record won't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 561, 601, as well pages 137, 168, and 169. There is not even a single piece of evidence that the SDS in Samac cooperated with JNA in Samac municipality. On the contrary, there is evidence that SDS and JNA were often at odds with one another. After all this, Your Honour, the Prosecution still maintains that the only reasonable inference for the creation of a Crisis Staff is that it was done pursuant to this document which cannot produce any which -- and which no one has seen. The Prosecution again raised the issue of the alleged -- of the alleged document -- just a moment. Of the alleged document this is Exhibit P71, yesterday on transcript page 33. Needless to say, the Defence thoroughly addressed the Prosecution document during the entire proceedings and in particular in its final brief and the closing arguments. Again the Defence draws the Trial Chamber's attention to the following facts: It is well established during the trial proceedings that more than one stamps of the Crisis Staff was in operation in that period, specifically the Trial Chamber witness, Mitar Mitrovic, secretary of Crisis Staff and of Serbian municipality, testified that there had been no special control over the stamp's utilisation, indicating the possibility of the stamp's misuse. All Defence witnesses, members of the Crisis Staff, as well as the other municipal officials who gave evidence before this Honourable Trial Chamber categorically denied that the Crisis Staff ever adopted this or any similar decision. This is a criminal trial. We have to see whether the level of reasonable doubt was reached by the Prosecution. They have the burden of proof. We cannot speculate to this. The evidence does not establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the signature belongs to Dr. Simic, which is explicitly confirmed by the Defence expert witness Professor Aleksic. The text of the decision is written in Latin script, and the Defence respectfully reminds once again that all decisions and acts of the Crisis Staff were written in Cyrillic alphabet. On the other hand, all other and decisions of the police, we have that in exhibits, were written exclusively in Latin alphabet. In addition to that, codefendant Zaric gave evidence that he had seen copies of this document in the police building allegedly which further proves, assuming that -- that he saw, that this is an entirely police and military matter, as Defence stated before. And finally, Your Honours, you can see on Exhibit P71, there is no title as usual, as it was in other Crisis Staff documents. It said only "Crisis Staff," municipal Crisis Staff. There is no -- a keyword which is often used here to blame my client, the keyword is the president. Compare this document P71 with the other documents, and you will see the word "president" is never -- it's not on the P71. And we addressed this particular issue in many details, Your Honours, in our brief, including the terms "vital objects" used in this particular document, and all other aspects and positions of the Defence. Your Honour, it seems that I'm almost at the end of my submission after two years of trial proceedings. Good moments, sad moments, that's the life of a lawyer, that's a part of trial proceedings. But if the time will permit, I will not now interfere with the submission of my learned friends. I would like to have a permission to express my gratitude to this Trial Chamber, to the participants, at the end of our submissions. Probably I would have a few minutes. But now, with regard to the sentencing, with regard to the proposal of Prosecution regarding Dr. Simic, they asked between 20 and 25 years of the prison. Dr. Simic, as I stated a million times here, he is not guilty. They did not respond to our questions, Your Honours, posed on the transcript on the record on the 1st of July. Many questions with regard to the particular mens rea of Dr. Simic, what he did, how he acted, and what was the atmosphere in Samac municipality. I addressed several matters with regard to the case law and other legal requirements in our brief with regard to the issue of possible sentencing, although Dr. Simic should be pronounced not guilty. This is a historic and unique chance, Your Honours, that these three men here should be acquitted, unique chance for the public opinion in former Yugoslavia, but we know that Croats were acquitted by this Tribunal, Muslims were acquitted. And frankly, I'm not entering into the analysis of the other cases. This is a unique historical chance, Your Honours, that these three defendants will be acquitted, first of all my client, of course. In conclusion, Your Honour, what I can say with regard to the issue of proposed sentence, I will tell you: 2003, Dr. Simic goes free. That is the position of the Defence, Your Honours. And I will say it in B/C/S language, because the spirit of the language is different, "[B/C/S spoken]." This is the position of the Defence. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. As I address the Trial Chamber today,, as I make my last submissions, I have to say something obviously with great delay because my client indicated this to me often during the trial, but I thought this was not that relevant, and I'm afraid that this is coming in very late, but I have to say this for the transcript. My client during these proceedings had terrible problems due to the fact that his last name is Tadic and that another indictee before this Tribunal had the same name, Tadic. So often when the name Tadic was used, this was reflected on my client. My client said to me several times that I should draw the attention of the Court to that, especially when legal issues were being discussed in the courtroom, I thought that we all knew who the Tadic who was being referred to was. But yesterday, when my learned friend spoke about the joint criminal enterprise of Tadic together with Knezevic, we all know who this is, but I wanted it to be reflected in the transcript that Miroslav Tadic has nothing to do with all these charges related to the Prijedor area. Now I wish to add something to what Mr. Pantelic said very briefly. In my final brief, I also raised a few questions asking the Prosecutor to get answers. But I did not give a -- get a single answer to my questions. I didn't hear any during their final submissions now, and I will expect to get these answers from the Trial Chamber. Now what is it that I wanted to know? I wanted to know certain things, but then the Prosecution did not respond to that. But obviously they highlighted other things that they attach importance to. First I'm going to say a few words about demographic experts Ewa Tabeau, the Prosecution expert, and also the word that obviously hurt the Prosecution, the word I used, and that was manipulation. The Prosecutor said yesterday that this was a minor error, and it was rectified, and then this showed the high professional level of their expert. This is a word that is a resounding one, manipulation, but I, as a layman, took it out of the expert opinion proffered by the Prosecution. I did not challenge this through evidence of my own. I took this from her evidence, from their analysis, from their Exhibit P131. This is not only a minor error, Your Honours, because this minor error has led to a major conclusion. It is analysis P133. And it was said that first Croats and Muslims constituted a significant part of the population of the municipality of Vukosavlje and then her tables and her analyses show that in the municipality of Odzak Vukosavlje in 1991, there were six Muslims. And she gave the figure of 2.250 originally, saying that Muslims lived in the municipality. And then when I put that question to her, whether this was an error, she said, "no, I did not take them into account." And then when I asked her again, then she said, "yes, I made a mistake." And she corrected her mistake. She corrected it, so that her credibility would not go down the drain completely, and it already had been brought into question. Our expert, Svetlana Radovanovic, did not say what Mr. Di Fazio said yesterday, that there were no ethnic changes in the composition of the population. She said something different. And this is what I referred to in my final brief and closing arguments, that there were no scrupulous, accurate sources of data that can give us the answer that is required. And then she said if we were to look at the entire territory, if the municipality had not been divided and also if certain settlements were not to be singled out, the divided settlements, then there would not have been drastic changes in the ethnic composition of the population. And she said that the analysis was not good because the sources were is not good. That's what our expert said. The problem lies elsewhere. Since we showed and proved that this method is bad and that the sources are bad, although our expert said that this method can be applied but not to this extent, not to discredit so many things and not to take them out of context to such an extent, then the Prosecution really had a big problem. Why? Because, Your Honours, this method and these sources are not the underlying thesis for Bosanski Samac in that case. It's not the case of Bosanski Samac that's a problem for them. Look at the expertise of Ewa Tabeau in the context of the Biljana Plavsic case and judgement, using the same methods, the same sources, and nobody challenged that expert opinion there. There was no cross-examination there. There was a guilty plea. The same expert, Ewa Tabeau, did this same expert opinion in the Naletelic case and the Galic case, that is the problem of the Prosecution. Because in the small Samac case, it was established that the sources were bad. This Trial Chamber and this Court has an important task that rulings cannot be made in criminal law on the basis of such poor sources and such poor evidence. We have offered other evidence to you, and you will certainly make your judicial assessment on that basis. Mrs. Radovanovic said to Judge Lindholm, if the sources were is good, if they were proper, can it be established when the population changed and she said quite clearly when this happened. We have sources from 1991 and 1997, and we have the indictment of 1991 and 1993. Now, what are we supposed to do, to say that everybody left in 1994? This would not be helpful to the Trial Chamber. It would not assist them. As for Esad Dagovic, I'm not going to squander my time on him. I think that the Zaric Defence counsel will speak about him, at least in a few words. May I just present our point of view with regard to that witness. This witness took that paper that everybody reads here before this Trial Chamber. He also made a solemn declaration claim. Read the statement of his father, read the statement of Fitozovic, and he said, "yes, the little waiter was a member of our SDA patrols." And this Esad Dagovic swore an oath before you here. Now, I would like to say a few other things. And then the Prosecution says that my client is lying. That's the way they linked all of this up. As for the letter to the patriarch, I wish to say a few words. First of all, I'm going to say that my client is a very religious man. You have heard testimony to that effect, you also have the deposition of a priest, and you have heard other evidence here. Would somebody compromise himself by making such claims and invoking the name of the patriarch? I know that the question that I've raised just now is not argumentation in a criminal trial. You all know what Tadic said. All witnesses who were members of the Crisis Staff say that this letter was not discussed at the Crisis Staff meeting. It is only the repenting Stevan Todorovic who has said otherwise, and something similar is said by the signatory of that letter Mitar Mitrovic. Witness Q confirmed during his examination-in-chief by the Prosecution, and also during the cross-examination, that Tadic told him about his conversation with the patriarch. Who is the Trial Chamber going to believe? Todorovic, Mitrovic, or Witness Q? Please read that part of the conversation in detail, what Witness Q said that Tadic had told him. What would Tadic's interest be in starting to testify about this particular subject if nobody had put him in the context of that letter except for the fact that at that time he was a member of the Crisis Staff, and this is also relevant in terms of other documents. Tadic wanted to tell the Trial Chamber something that he had experienced, something that he is proud of, he is proud of having spoken to the patriarch, and he is proud of the fact that he conveyed parts of this conversation to other people, and he is proud of how he told Mitrovic and Todorovic about that. It is somebody else who should bow their heads in relation to that letter. As for the other alleged lie told by my client, that he took part in the events of the 17th of April by collecting weapons, had the Prosecution heard properly what I said, and I had said that Tadic did not participate at all in anything that happened between the 16th and 17th of April, that's what he said and he did not lie. Tadic took part in the collection of weapons, and he did not lie. Where did he lie? This was on the 18th. And this was confirmed by witnesses, first and foremost, his commander, Radovan Antic who said that on the 18th, of the morning, he told him to collect weapons or to take part in supervising weapons collection in the Fourth Quarter. Zasavica was mentioned yesterday as well, whether this transfer had taken place in May or in August. We indeed have the testimony of Jelena Kapetanovic who was in Crkvina, and she said that part of the women from neighbouring villages were transferred to Zasavica in the month of May. That is what Petar Karlovic said as well, that he heard some families were transferred to Zasavica. Pasaga Tihic, whose name the Prosecution invoked, did not say that. He just said that people were taken from the village and Zasavica is mentioned in that context. But it was not said that they were taken to Zasavica. Again, I'm going to remind you of Witness Q. In response to the questions put by the Prosecution and the Defence, he said that 4.500 inhabitants of Croat villages, precisely these villages, Hasici, Novo Selo, Tisina, left that territory on the 16th, 17th, and 18th of April. That he went through his parish, and he did not see anyone except for soldiers, not a single person who had been transferred to Zasavica in May. There was no one there. There were these 400 to 500 men, and he himself said that Stjepan Blazanovic took about 250, and 250 were detained. That's what he said. You will read his statement. What I heard yesterday from Mr. Weiner is what I really wanted to hear, exactly. All these documents that I referred to, as well as Mr. Weiner, show that there is organisation in forced labour or rather work obligation. It is correct, there is a link between the Executive Board, the Ministry of Defence, and the secretariat for the economy and other secretariats. That is what I claimed, but that's not what they claimed in their final brief. They claimed something completely different. They claimed that Miroslav Tadic was at the top of the pyramid of forced labour, number one. But that's not what they said yesterday. Now, what did they say yesterday? It is correct, this is who did this, the Ministry of Defence, and their other beneficiaries or rather secretariats in cooperation with the Executive Board. It was not the civilian protection staff that was involved there. It is the way we had said it was. Yes, they addressed the Ministry of Defence and they asked for people from the work brigade. They asked for specialised glass cutters so that the window panes could be changed, yes. Is that what he is guilty of, that glass was put on window panes in houses in Samac? And do you know what happened after that? They realised that it was useless to put glass because all the windows crumbled, so then they put plastic sheets, that's what they did. Yes. And then upon instructions of the Executive Board in accordance with document D113/3, they took glass from Uniglas, Uniglas is a glass factory. They did not take it off houses and roofs the way the Prosecution has been trying to put it. There is no evidence to that effect, nobody said that, not even their witness Nusret Hadzijusufovic who was their witness with regard to forced labour. The Prosecution remained disarmed with regard to their thesis on forced labour. They did not present a shred of evidence to the effect that my client and his civilian protection staff had anything to do with forced labour. It was work obligation that was conducted according to procedure. Again, may I say that yesterday we heard a thesis of the Prosecution, and what we heard from Mr. Re is something that I understand in the following way: Cooperation with the Prosecution exists only if an accused person makes a confession. But it's not important to tell the truth; it is important that they say what I, the Prosecutor, am interested in having them say, what I can use in order to prove my own case. That is what they call cooperation. No. It is for the Trial Chamber so assess who cooperated with the Office of the Prosecutor. It is not for them to say. The Court knows that my client provided the Office of the Prosecution with 60 documents, and they used them in their case. The Court knows that my client gave an interview, that they introduced into evidence and that they showed to witnesses when they wanted to shake them. You know that Miroslav Tadic said such and such a thing in his interview. That's the way they would put it. Gentlemen of the Prosecution, did this perhaps not suit you in terms of important cooperation? This Trial Chamber will assess what meaningful cooperation is in terms of quantity, quality, and whether there were some interests. There is clear jurisprudence in this respect from the Blaskic case, the Kordic case, I think there was quite a bit of reference that was made to that. Your Honours, after 234 days, I conclude my submissions to this Court. I just wish to say a few more words. May I say that it is not all the same to me, although I've made every effort to be a professional, but I do want to say a few words regarding my own attitude towards this Court and towards my client. In the country that I come from, judgements are passed on behalf of the people, in the name of the people. That is how the preamble of a judgement starts, like in many other countries I presume. Your Honours, you are passing judgement on behalf of the international community. Your mandate was given to you on behalf of the entire world. You are passing judgement on behalf of the international community. You are trying people under the same flag under which Miroslav Tadic served in Sinai in 1960. He believed deeply when he surrendered to this Court that the Court, this Honourable Trial Chamber that has had highest mandate, this paramount mandate from the international community will fairly and justly weigh all the evidence and the story he had to tell. I must say that personally, as a professional and as Defence counsel, I'm convinced of that. In conclusion, may I ask the Trial Chamber whether it would be possible for our clients to address the Trial Chamber if they wish to do so after these 234 days. I believe that they deserve that. May I just say one more thing, that it has been a professional honour, a great professional honour for myself and for my colleague Mr. Krgovic to represent persons before this Court and that everything that I heard and learned here is something that I hope I will be able to draw on in my practice, and I will be pleased if at least part of the legal efforts we made will leave some trace before this Tribunal. I wish to thank you, and I think that I have to say one more thing. I think I have to apologise to the interpreters for all the things they said to me and to my colleague Mr. Krgovic over these past two years. Two days ago, they said to me that I finally slowed down and started speaking at a proper pace. And Mr. Tadic also objected when he said, Why is my Defence attorney in such a hurry? I also which to wish Mr. Krgovic and I also wish to thank our assistants who were so helpful in these proceedings. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Pisarevic or Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Zaric will very briefly give its reply to certain allegations of the Prosecution and to some position that the Prosecution made clear in their reply to our closing arguments. But before that, I would first to reply to something that Mr. Pantelic has just said regarding political positions of Mr. Zaric and positions of Mr. Blagoje Simic. And I can confirm, it is the truth that Mr. Zaric and Mr. Zaric [sic] were and still are political opponents. That's true, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mentioned the two names. You said Mr. Zaric and Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric and Mr. Simic, Blagoje Simic. I apologise. But the fact that they were political opponents was not the reason that Mr. Zaric gave his evidence the way he did. Mr. Zaric testified before this Tribunal under oath in order to give evidence of events that happened in Bosanski Samac in 1992 in order to tell the truth, and this is the only reason that his evidence is the way it is. It has nothing to do with his political positions, with his participation in the political party which is opponents to SDS. Mr. Di Fazio, talking about credibility of certain witnesses, mentioned Witness Esad Dagovic, and as my dear colleague Mr. Lukic said, I will address the Trial Chamber the credibility of this witness because I believe that this is very characteristic situation regarding this witness. Mr. Di Fazio tried to explain some contradictions in the evidence of this evidence saying that it is easy to confuse a tank with an APC, and that it has been ten years since the incidents occurred back in 1992. And it is true what Mr. Di Fazio said. It is easy for someone who is not a military person to confuse a tank or an APC, and it is true that it has been ten years since it happened. But this is not the issue. The issue related to the credibility of this witness is not whether he could recognise a difference between a tank and an APC, but the issue is why this witness said that on 17 of April, he went for a brief period to pizzeria, together with Hasan Bicic, that he had breakfast with Hasan and Muhamed Bicic, and then he returned home and remained at his home during this whole day. Why did he say that? Or rather, why Witness Kemal Mehinovic, Prosecution witness, on page 7572 and 73 said that he saw Esad Dagovic armed with an automatic rifle in front of the building so-called Carrington building in Bosanski Samac with a group of other Muslim men, also armed with automatic rifles. Why would Prosecution Witness Kemal Mehinovic say that? Why would father of Esad and Safet Dagovic said - we have this in document C1 - that both his sons participated in fighting during the 17 of April, and that they returned to their document in early morning of 18 of April. These are the issues of importance for the credibility of Witness Esad Dagovic. And not just for the testimony of Witness Esad Dagovic, also for the testimony and the evidence of witnesses Hasan Bicic, Muhamed Bicic, Hasan Subasic, and Witness M. None of these witnesses didn't want to admit that they participated in resistance, that they had been organised, and that on the 17 of April they offered resistance to Serb paramilitaries. To be honest, I'm not blaming them for that. All right, they heard shots. They saw that something is happening in town. They took their weapons and went out to offer resistance. But why they lied before this Tribunal that they were at their homes and they didn't do it, this is the question that the Trial Chamber should ask itself. One issue that Mr. Re raised in his reply is in relation to Mr. Zaric's book. Mr. Re suggested that Mr. Zaric, during his evidence, should have pointed all the inconsistencies and all the mistakes that he made in his books. What we would like to say, that the examination-in-chief of Mr. Zaric lasted for full seven days of valuable and expensive trial time. Going through each and every paragraph of Mr. Zaric's book would take -- under our estimation, it would take at least two or three more days. And I don't believe that this Trial Chamber would allow us to do that. It is -- it was our impression. Mr. Zaric himself in his evidence said and pointed to a few examples regarding dates, events, names, et cetera, that are incorrect in his book. We thought it was enough for the Trial Chamber to have a clear picture about what weight should be given to such an evidence. I don't want the Trial Chamber to get the wrong impression that Mr. Zaric is ashamed of his book. He's not. Quite the contrary, he is very proud on his book. Mr. Zaric would like just to say that, and he said already in his evidence here, that the book was written in Ekavian dialect, the dialect that he does not use, that the introduction of his book is quite the opposite from his political positions, written by a person who doesn't share the same political ideals as Mr. Zaric. There was an example that Mr. Maxim Simeunovic who was a witness here, was referred there as Maksimovic in this book, and then there was one omission regarding the date of the incident in Crkvina, 7th or 8th of May. So just to give some examples of some inconsistencies with his book. When Mr. Zaric wrote his book, it wasn't his intention that his book should be evidence in any legal proceedings. Having in mind that Mr. Zaric was warned by the Prosecution on three occasions when he gave interviews that everything he said can be used against him in the proceedings, as well as the fact that Mr. Zaric testified here under oath that he gave a solemn declaration, the value of these evidence, meaning interviews of Mr. Zaric and his evidence before the Trial Chamber, is far greater than one Romanesque view of the events that happened. The Trial Chamber shouldn't give the weight, the probative value, to Mr. Zaric's book greater than the value given to those written by Mr. Sulejman Tihic, Dragan Delic, Dragan Lukac, and some other witnesses. Their books this Trial Chamber didn't want to admit into evidence. And in particular regarding the allegation of the Prosecution that the book of Mr. Zaric is the best evidence of cooperation between Serbian government and the JNA, we would like to draw the Trial Chamber's interest to one particular chapter of Mr. Zaric's book. And it is called "Hymn to the Army." It speaks for itself. Your Honours, is it time for us to take our usual break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will take our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just a few more words regarding Mr. Zaric's book, the importance of messages sent to the public through Mr. Zaric's book is the condemnation of crimes, ethnic intolerance, and all other bad things that happened in Bosanski Samac, and that the only right way to understand Mr. Zaric's book. The Defence is very pleased with the Prosecutor's position that the book of Mr. Zaric should be read in its entirety because this is the only it could be understood in a proper way. His book was highly valuated, relevant persons in Yugoslavia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the main thing about this book is its contribution in order to reunite people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the courage to condemn all the bad things committed by people of his own ethnicity. The Prosecution suggested that from the fact that Mr. Zaric saw Document P71 in three offices in police station, it can be concluded that he was a chief of national security in Bosanski Samac. The mere presence of Mr. Zaric in police station, of course, cannot be used to make a conclusion that he carried any official post within the police, as the Prosecution is trying to suggest. Without any wish to elaborate more on this fact, the Defence of Mr. Zaric could give a couple of examples of what Mr. Zaric could have done in the police station. He could have had a coffee with his acquaintance; he could have gone there to extend his driving license validity, his ID validity, or for whatever other reason. It seems that the Prosecution didn't understand fully what Mr. Pisarevic said in his closing arguments regarding the role of legally elected government and the role of Yugoslav People's Army in all this. What Mr. Pisarevic said is that in all parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which municipal governments were replaced by some other governments, for example, Crisis Staff or whatever, the JNA didn't intervene in order to re-establish the previous government. And it made no difference to the JNA whether these newly established governments or authorities were Bosniak, Croat, or Serb. The JNA didn't intervene in Odzak when the Crisis Staff took over. The JNA didn't intervene in Tuzla, in Mostar, in Livno, in Bugojno, in Vitez, where Croat-dominated or Muslim-dominated Crisis Staffs took over. And this was the real meaning of what Mr. Pisarevic said. The position of JNA was not to intervene and not to interfere in such occurrences. And just a few more words regarding the lack -- alleged lack of cooperation of Mr. Zaric with the Prosecution. Having in mind that Mr. Re said that the Prosecution through myself wanted to talk to Mr. Zaric, and of course that Mr. Pisarevic was informed in that respect because he wasn't in The Hague at that time, I have to admit that it is true what Mr. Re said. But in order to give some more light on this episode, I believe that the Trial Chamber is entitled to have a full information on this. Of course, I will not break the confidentiality of my talks with the Prosecution, and I will not give any detail that might jeopardise the confidentiality of our talks. But I believe I'm not doing this by saying that it was initiated by the Prosecution in order to try to find if there is any possibility of plea bargaining with Mr. Zaric. This was not a formal request of the Prosecution to have an additional interview with Mr. Zaric; it was a call for plea bargaining. After informing Mr. Zaric about the details of the proposal, he said that he will never admit his guilt for any of the crimes as they are stated in the indictment and that his position hasn't changed since 1998 when first letter sent by the Prosecution with a proposal for a plea bargain. He said he's not guilty, he doesn't feel guilty, and he cannot say that he's guilty for something that he hasn't done. And from this point of view, since the Defence doesn't see that plea bargain negotiation are same thing as lack of cooperation, namely that the Prosecution asked for interview with Mr. Zaric and that he refused it, he believe that we said the truth when we said that the Prosecution didn't want to talk to Mr. Zaric. At the end, regarding this same issue, the Defence of Mr. Zaric has to say something that believes deeply, and this is that the sentencing recommendation of the Prosecution is some sort of revenge for Mr. Zaric's position regarding his plea bargain. A few more words about personal notes of Mr. Zaric that were mentioned here, during cross-examination of Mr. Zaric, Mr. Re had the opportunity to ask Mr. Zaric whether he wants to hand over his personal notes or not. Just that simple question. Mr. Re didn't do it. So the position of Mr. Zaric's Defence is that is unfair that the Prosecutor's final brief, this alleged lack of cooperation - I apologise - should be considered as such when Mr. Re never actually asked for these personal notes, nor Mr. Re, nor the Trial Chamber, would never know what the answer of Mr. Zaric would be. At the end, I would like on behalf of Mr. Pisarevic and myself to say that it was our great privilege to be Defence counsel in this case before this Honourable Trial Chamber and to express our gratitude to all the members of our team, including Ms. Maja Dokmanovic, our case manager, to everybody they contributed in the Defence of Mr. Zaric. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could be in a situation to address the Trial Chamber only a few minutes because I mentioned during my submission that I would like to express my personal honour on behalf of my Defence teams acting before this Trial Chamber and in this Tribunal. But before that, Your Honour, please just allow me for the record to mention a number of footnotes where the Defence, footnotes of the Prosecution brief, where the Defence find some serious inconsistencies, so it maybe assist the Trial Chamber in their evaluation of the parties' submissions. Namely these are the footnotes from the OTP's brief 66, 98, 99, 154, 206, 244, 246, 276, 314, 363, 440, 553, 826, and 891. There are some technical errors, but there are some substantial issues and sort of errors which are of the importance for the evaluation of the case in its totality. So thank you very much for your attention. And Your Honour, on behalf of Dr. Simic's Defence team, I would like to express my great honour that I was able to act before this Honourable Trial Chamber and in this Honourable Tribunal. Throughout this period of more than 200 hearing days, all of us here in this courtroom worked very hard, to the best of our abilities. Also, I would like to express my great honour and my gratitude to our learned friends from the Prosecution bench. They worked vigorously, they really presented their case in a highly professional manner. While the role of the Defence is to challenge the Prosecution case, and finally the Trial Chamber will decide, but as I said, speaking on behalf of all Defence teams in this case, it was a great, really great privilege to work with our friends from the Prosecution bench. We learned a lot from them. They are well-experienced, common-law lawyers. It was a great experience for us coming from continental law system, civil-law system. And also we learned a lot from their mistakes, because we are Defence, and then we are trying to make manoeuvring area for our case. And I also would like to thank them for both of the contributions. Then, Your Honour, we would like to express our gratitude to the members of the registry and to the members of the court department, court officers acting in this case. They were enormously favourable to us in many of the issues, technical issues, procedural issues, out of hearing hours, and that was a great privilege and a great honour for us to meet and to work with such decent and highly professional colleagues. Also, I would like to express my great honour and gratitude to the hard work of the interpretation unit, our friends from interpreters' booths. I know that they were in many occasions in so stressful situations that certain presentation or positions of the parties were, and then they try always to resolve these matters and to inform us in order to have a clear picture, clear transcript, and finally to have actually a proper case. So again, I really would like to thank to all of them. Also, I would like to express our gratitude to the colleagues from the technical booth, video unit, and other services. We met a lot of them. Also, needless to say that members of victims and witness unit are also, in our eyes, one of the keystones of the work of the Tribunal in order to prepare everything that the trial can go on. They were enormously professional with regard to the witnesses, in regard to the arrangements, with regard to the passports, visas, and many, many very serious issues that the Defence and as well as Prosecution faced in order to present their case. And also, the Defence would like to express our gratitude to all members of security unit, to all members -- all officers of security department of the Tribunal, as well as UN Detention Unit with the head of the Detention Unit, Commander Mr. Tim McFadden. They help us in every aspect of our work whenever it was necessary to meet the client in the detention facilities within the Tribunal, whenever it was necessary to help us in many, many other aspects of our daily life and our daily work. And finally, Your Honours, allow me to address another matter with regard to the media coverage of this particular case. We know what is the role of the Tribunal. We know what is the importance of the Tribunal, and we know what is the influence of the work of the Tribunal for the restoration of peace and multiethnic relations in former Yugoslavia. Practically all members of media working here as professionals did their job highly professionally, highly professionally. I must outline that technical units of the Tribunal and via satellite through the network B92 for Belgrade, at least in Serbia, the public opinion can be afforded the possibility to follow live coverage. However, Your Honours, I must say- I'm speaking on behalf of my team - maybe the other colleagues will support my submission - I must say that the network or the agency Sense working here is highly unprofessional. It's editor in chief, Mr. Mirko Klarin, who is solely responsible for the creation of the coverage of the cases within this Tribunal showed, and it can be found on internet pages, everyone can check what is the nature and what is the quality of the coverage of Sense agency here. Let me give you a few examples. Our friends --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I don't think that this is the proper forum for that. If you have any complaints, please address them to the Office of the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any complaints. I'm finishing in 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What I would like to say in terms of the role of the Tribunal and in terms of the very great importance of the media coverage, of the work of the Tribunal, I just want to outline, and I hope that agency Sense, which is more maybe we can call nonsense, can change their attitude towards the presentation of the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are again going into what I said this is not the proper forum. Will you please sit down. I think you are finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I hope that Sense agency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please sit down, Mr. Pantelic. The Trial Chamber was asked to allow the accused persons to address the Trial Chamber directly, and the Trial Chamber has accepted to do that. And will give any of the accused who want to address the Chamber ten minutes, hoping that they will restrict themselves to matters involved in this case that is before the Trial Chamber. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, just very, very briefly, thank you for making that clear, if Your Honours please, there's no provision for this procedure in the rules. I just want to say that the Prosecution would object to this course of action. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, there's no express provision in the rules. But there is nothing to stop the Trial Chamber to allow the accused persons themselves to speak if they so wish. As this is their case, they are the accused persons. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So I'll ask Dr. Simic if he wants to say anything. You're not compelled to say anything. It's just that there was a request before the Trial Chamber. THE ACCUSED SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the end of this trial, I wish to express my deepest sympathy with all the victims of the unhappy civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1992 to 1995. I wish to thank all the participants in these legal proceedings. I wish to thank Their Honours for their patience in hearing out all of us who had something to say. I wish to thank the technical services for their professional work. I wish to thank my Defence counsel for their patience in understanding my high expectations from them. I cannot thank the Prosecutors because they did not act correctly. But I can thank them because I learned a lot from them. Although I entered these proceedings without any legal knowledge whatsoever, I learned from them all the time. The lack of correctness in relation to me manifested itself in the presentation of many falsehoods, many half-truths and manipulations. My Defence revealed this many times and directed Their Honours toward the truth and the truth in this unhappy conflict. I will add only one more thing referring directly to the proceedings, that it is nothing new when I say that only those who have weapons have power in a wartime situation. That is only those who use weapons. I, dressed the way I was, had no power during the war, and I had no authority. I never hit, killed, or raped anyone, nor did I ever see anyone doing such things. I never asked anyone else to do such things. I do not hate anyone, and I have never hated anyone. I hold no grudge against anybody. I am convinced that the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina, although they warred among themselves many times throughout history and had many conflicts in the past, will today find a way of living together without this ever leading to war again. I'm convinced that this last lesson they learned from this war will teach them to find ways of living together. But I'm also convinced that the arbiters in such agreement and negotiations can never be communists. I would also like to take this opportunity to apologise for several emotional outbursts that I had before this Trial Chamber. I reacted emotionally several times and lost control of my emotions. This is not how I am usually, but this combination of half-truths, manipulations, and lies led me to that kind of reaction for which I apologise. And thank you again for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Miroslav Tadic, if you wish to address the Trial Chamber. THE ACCUSED TADIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be very brief. All these apologies and all this praise, that is, everything that my Defence counsel said is something I support and will not repeat now. Jesus said: "Let him who is without sin cast the first stone" and nobody cast a stone. It is not my intention to defend myself now because so much has been said here, and the material is so voluminous that this would not be possible. It is up to you to reach a judgement. Your Honours, I have to say a few words about something into which I have invested a lot of effort, knowledge, and, I might say, all of myself. That is the exchanges. I was wholly engrossed in that, and I am still preoccupied with it. I thought I was doing something humane, helping people in distress. And the Prosecution position has not caused me to waver in that conviction. A lot of work has been done on this by my counsel, and I might add some people were killed doing that job, such as, for example, Mr. Drljanic from Bosanski Brod. There are still many missing persons whose fates are not known. Many families are still waiting to hear news of their nearest and dearest, even if the news is that they are dead. During my provisional release, I did a lot, but not enough because I was limited in my movements. While staying at home, I had the opportunity to meet quite a lot of people, the people who are mentioned in these proceedings. Namik Suljic, whom you have heard about here; Galib Nurkic; Stipo Dragicevic; Djuro Krajinovic; Goja with the children; Mensur Tubakovic, also known as Pipa; Marko Prgomet; Beba Salkic, the sister of Ibrahim Salkic who recently got married to a relative of mine. All of them, whether they were exchanged or left in some other way, treated me in a very friendly way, and I treated them the same. I have enumerated only a few because the list of those who came to share their reminiscences with me is very long, reminiscences from those dreadful times. Your Honours, the commissions are still working, and they will still have a lot to do on searching for missing persons. This will go on for a long time. Commissions on all the warring sides are still working on this. And my assistance will be very useful to them, whatever the time when I'm able to leave The Hague. I will not speak about where my colleagues are who worked in the commissions, and many of them are still working there. My counsel spoke of this. On Wednesday, the 2nd of July of this year, an exchange was carried out, or rather a handover, between the previously warring sides, and this took place on the border of the newly created countries, an exchange of corpses. Your Honours, a wise man once said that if somebody's holding a hammer in their hand, everything looks like a nail to them. It was the Prosecution that held this hammer. I cannot escape the impression that the Prosecution considers anyone sitting in this bench a criminal. Fortunately, there is also a Trial Chamber. The only thing I have ever been punished for is parking in the wrong place. All this looks surreal to me, it looks impossible. All my knowledge of courts comes from films I have seen on television. In these films, something usually happens at the last moment leading to a happy end. I hope the same will happen in these proceedings before this Tribunal. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Simo Zaric. THE ACCUSED ZARIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, participants in these proceedings, I have only a few words to say. I'm deeply convinced that only truth can lead to justice, and this was the motto under which I operated when I surrendered to The Hague Tribunal. These very long trial proceedings and my many years of abstaining from liberty never caused me any temptation that I could not come through. My cooperation with the Tribunal and especially the Prosecution was evident, and what weight and value this Trial Chamber will attach to this is something I leave to the Trial Chamber with full respect. Of course, I am deeply disappointed and angry because my sincere cooperation was denigrated by the Prosecution, which based many of their theses on this cooperation. Long ago, in 1998, on the 24th of February, I said, in front of several thousand citizens of Bosanski Samac seeing me off to The Hague, that I was going there with courage and determination in order to defend the honour and dignity of my nation and my family and myself as a human being. At the end of these proceedings, more than ever before in my life, I'm convinced that I have fulfilled this honourable task fully and honourably. I wish to say that I'm an atheist, but I do not mock believers. I respect their religious feelings fully. My religion, my faith, my conviction in this drama I am going through are placed only in you, Your Honours. I trust that you will reach the most just decision. What could incite honourable people, honest people, such as I was during the war, should such a situation, God forbid, ever arise again, what would happen if people like me had not been around? There would have been many more victims. The suffering would have been much greater. In my view, this would have been a tragedy. Punishment of several years in prison is not a tragedy, in my view, nor is everything I went through together with my family for the last five years. The greatest tragedy for Simo Zaric would be to be branded a war criminal for the rest of my life. I and my family would have to bear this brand through the rest of our lives. But we have put forward arguments and honourable and true testimonies to disprove this. No sentence can make a nationalist of me, nor can it cause me to deviate from my path in life. That is why I wrote this book. I beg you to read it from cover to cover. It is not evidence in legal terms. What I wanted to say in this book can be understood only if you read it from cover to cover, rather than reading just extracts pulled out of context by those who accuse me. That is why, Your Honours, I am deeply convinced that you will reach the only right decision, which is that I am not guilty and release me to enjoy the freedom I deserve together with my family because I have done what I did. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have now come to the end of our proceedings, and this is the close of the proceedings in this trial. The Trial Chamber will deliberate on the evidence and on the submissions, and the date of judgement will be notified to the parties. The Court will rise.
